newsitem.title: USA: Capital gains tax cut buoys U.S. stocks near term.
newsitem.headline: Capital gains tax cut buoys U.S. stocks near term.

text.p: Speculation about a cut in the capital gains tax on profits from the sale of securities is likely to create a near term "bubble" in the U.S. stock market and then some choppiness when the cut actually becomes effective, traders and analysts said.
Analysts noted the details of a tax cut are unknown at the moment, although all agreed some reduction was in the offing.
"Our view is that there is a very good chance we'll get a budget deal this year, including a capital gains tax cut," said Arun Kumar, strategist at Lehman Brothers.

Hugh Johnson, market strategist at First Albany Co, said a cut in the capital gains tax could take the form of cutting the rate to perhaps around 20 percent, or excluding a portion of the capital gain. Another widely discussed idea is to have the profit indexed to the inflation rate through some formula.
"The real issue, to me, is the holding period requirement," Johnson said.

Lawmakers in the give and take of negotiation could exclude securities held for a short interval from favorable tax treatment and perhaps require that stocks be held for years to get the maximum benefit.

The Securities Industry Association (SIA), trade group for brokers and investment banks, has called for a 50 percent reduction in the capital gains tax. Currently, the top personal rate is 28 percent.
Virtually every analyst and trader agreed the immediate effect of all the speculation is that some people will put off selling until they can see exactly what the changes are.
"It will create a short term bubble," said one trader, who agreed less stock for sale would contribute to higher prices.

William LeFevre, analyst at Ehrenkrantz King Nussbaum said some people might decide to lock in the benefit of a lower tax rate by selling shares short now and then delivering the stock when the tax cut is set into law.
While the analysts agreed the boost to share prices near term would probably be followed by a burst of selling on the effective date, no one saw a disastrous drop in stock prices.
Kumar said people hold stocks for a particular reason and "unless that reason changes there is not going to be a deluge fo selling just because capital gains taxes have been cut."

LeFevre said a practical piece of advice for people to remember is that "if you let the tax collector influence your investment strategy you're usually going to lose out somewhere along the way." He said the overall impact of any reduction will likely be neutral.
One trader noted that professional money managers who decide how to invest vast sums are influenced by the prices of securities, not by taxes.

Jeffrey Swarz, a CS First Boston analyst who tracks biotechnology stocks, said stock groups that traditionally offer the possibility of high capital appreciation rather than fat dividends would be relatively more attractive if the capital gains tax is cut. He said biotech group should now get an overweight rating instead of a neutral rating. He cited several large capitalization biotechs he is recommending, including Amgen Inc, Biogen Inc, Centocor Inc and Genzyme Corp. None of the four pays a regular dividend.

Perrin Long, an analyst who tracks the securities industry, said a capital gains tax cut would be a boon for the securities industry only if boosts the number of transactions that take place. While there could be some temporary influence on transactions, over time, factors like interest rates, the perception of the economy, the musings of technical analysts and corporate earnings all helped drive transactions.
